utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic, have you been seen by a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NALETILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I had a scan, my lungs, my neck. I wasn't seen by a doctor, though. We are waiting for the report, and then they will call me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. How are you feeling now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NALETILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same, the same as before. No change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Take care of yourself. You may sit down. I would like to draw the parties' attention to some changes in the trial schedule for the coming weeks. Mr. Seric, this might be particularly interesting for you to schedule the visits of your client's family with the registrar. Tomorrow afternoon session will start at 3.00 because of the Kupreskic appeal judgment. So we have to start a little bit late. As you know, on Wednesday, October 24th, there is a UN holiday, so there will be no court session. On Monday, October 29th, the next status conference in the Milosevic case. Due to security reasons, no other trial will be held on that day. Therefore, we will not sit on October 29th. Notwithstanding a possible change of the trial hours due to the outcome of the medical report on Mr. Naletilic's status of health, which we'll receive as of November the 1st, we'll sit in the first and second week of November during the regular court hours. In the third week of November, due to the arrival of the new Judges, there are some changes on the 22nd and the 23rd of November. On Thursday, 22nd, we will sit only from 9.30 to 12.00, in the morning. In the afternoon, the new Judges will give their solemn declaration in this courtroom. On Friday, November 23rd, an extraordinary plenary will take place in the morning. We will, therefore, not sit on that day. In December, we will sit during the normal court days in the first week of December. In the second week, there is a plenary from Wednesday, the 12th, until Friday, the 14th. We will, therefore, only be able to sit on December 10th and 11th in the second week of December. The Christmas Court recess starts on December 17th. The Tribunal will be recessed until January the 4th, 2002. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I take it -- I don't have a calendar in front of me. I apologise. Does that effectively mean that the 11th of December will be our last court day before Christmas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so, for this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the 29th of October, there being no court on that Monday, I wonder whether the Court would entertain having a full Court day on Friday to help make up for that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure at this moment. I have to consult with my colleagues concerning the time schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Poriouvaev will be handling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to discuss some questions relevant to our next witness in private session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will go to the private session. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question. Perhaps we didn't understand very well. Are we starting tomorrow at 3.00 or is the break prolonged until 3.00 tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The break will be prolonged until 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: The witness who is called -- sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in the open session. Witness, you may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, your request for protective measures has been granted by the Trial Chamber. You will have a pseudonym and you will be called in the Court Witness BB or Witness Double B, and you also will have facial distortion. Now the usher will give you a sheet of paper. You should read it but don't read it aloud, and if everything is all right, you may say yes or no, if your name is correctly spelled and your birthday is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Shall I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness BB, did you have any military training in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The school for reserve officers in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did you have this training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1976. The training was six months long, and then I went for additional training in the rank of -- in the rank of sergeant, interim sergeant. And then after I got out, I had five or six drills, because that was the system in the former Yugoslavia. So I eventually got the rank of reserve captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you belong to any military formation in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, from the beginning of July, I belonged to an HVO unit, the 4th Battalion more precisely, the group for maintenance of facilities. The command was at Rondo, and I spent three months in Tihomir Misic Barracks, located on the left bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the outset, in the barracks, it was a certain Mr. Mikolic and then he was replaced by a new commander whom I don't remember, and the commander of the 4th Battalion was Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long did you remain within the 4th Battalion of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remained in the 4th Battalion of the HVO until the attack on the Vranica building on the 9th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you recount what happened on the 9th of May in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the year was 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived on the Vranica building on the second floor which had a view of the School of Economics. Below me was the entrance to the command of the Mostar Brigade on the right-hand side; and on the left-hand side, there was the command of the BH army corps. Around 1500 hours, an UNPROFOR tank, which was located at the intersection of Stjepan Radica and Ante Zvonica Streets, and it had been standing there for 10 or 15 days already, because tensions were growing between the BH army and the HVO, was this located. And since I wake up very easily, I heard the tank move and leave. Around 10 to 5.00, the first grenade hit the room where I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: We will stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show the witness Exhibit Number P11.8 and get ready Exhibits 16.4 and 16.5, I mean P exhibits, of course. Mr. Usher, place Exhibit Number 11.8 on the ELMO. There is something wrong with the monitor, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just take this opportunity to ask you whether the transcript, which shows that around 1500 hours, the UNPROFOR tank, do you mean that's 3.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was 3.00 a.m., 3.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The audio/video booth just informed me that something is wrong with the ELMO and they are fixing it in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can do without the exhibits maybe at this point, unfortunately. I would like the Trial Chamber to see something more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope it could be fixed during the break. Okay, sure, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, then in the circumstances, we should proceed with the testimony. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first shell from a hand-held launcher, shooting started from all sides, from infantry weapons, from anti-aircraft cannons, from I don't know what else. All the tenants in the building, which is 11 floors high, ran down to the cellar to find shelter because they didn't know what was going on. Down in the cellar we remained that entire day, the 9th, the entire night between the 9th and the 10th, and the day of the 10th until 11.00 when HVO units arrived and took control of the cellar, captured the cellar. Of course, the tenants ran back to their apartments. Then through a public address system, the commander of the ATG group, anti-terrorist group, Juka Prazina, made an announcement and asked the army to surrender. There were about 10 soldiers who took off their uniforms and put on civilian clothes. Then one gentleman talked to Juka Prazina also through the public address system on behalf of the civilians and said that both the civilians and those soldiers who took off their uniforms would, indeed, surrender and get out. At that moment, three floors, three top-most floors and two floors -- two first floors were already burning on the side of the School of Economics, and the -- it was becoming insufferable inside the building. And judging by the -- after the conversation between Juka Prazina and this gentleman who spoke on behalf of the civilians, they agreed, and the civilians began leaving the building. We got out into Radica Street where we were met by Jusuf Juka with his fighting men --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will you stop here for a moment because the ELMO is all right now. We can use our exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So Exhibit P11.18, I see here. It's a map. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have P11.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: 18, I'm sorry. It's a mistake. Awfully sorry for that. You may place the map of Mostar on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness BB, would you indicate on the map the place where Vranica building was located? Just indicate it with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vranica building was located right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just for the record, please, name the street.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stjepan Radica Street, and there was a small street here by the name of Spojna between the School of Economics, which is located here, and the Vranica building, which is located here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Would you just draw a sketch of the building with the marker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The School of Economics, this is Vranica, this is the extension of these buildings, and this here is the School of Economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You may just put "BB" on the sketch. You indicated Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please approach the microphone when questioning? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now I ask you to place on the ELMO Exhibit number P16.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, what depicts this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Vranica building after the attack of the Croatian Defence Council that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. Now you may place Exhibit 16.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Which part of the building is it? I mean, there is some entrance to the building. To which area does it lead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the corps command and this was to the

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you probably understand what I'm trying to say. He was -- the witness was only supposed to show the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness BB, did you participate in the defence of the building along with army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not participate. I was with the other civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know Juka Prazina before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not personally. I knew him from sight. He had come to Mostar a number of times to Banovac and other places, but it was a name that was well -- Balinovac. It was a well-known name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was Juka's unit or his soldiers the only ones you saw in the street on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When we were all brought to the yard of the School of Economics, which was facing the avenija -- I saw Colonel Zelijko Bosnjak from the Convicts Battalion with six or seven of his soldiers. They were standing off to the side, and they had a red, white and blue insignia. Juka's fighters were in front of us. Juka had brought out all the young ones out, and five or six of us who were a bit older. He first asked whether there were any civilians among them. There were some. He told them to go home. The others whom they did not separate out had to go to the Velez stadium, which is at the Bijeli Brijeg. He kept us there for about two hours. He checked our documents. That is, his fighters did. If they found any money in wallets, they took that money. Then after that, in a column, two by two, he led us through on to Ante Zvonica Street, to the HVO ministry. This is what it was called at that time. That was in the old building of the Zagreb Bank, and there we were met by Tuta, Misic, Primorac, commander, I believe, of the corps. There were another 100 men in uniform there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, would you point and just answer my question. You just told that you saw -- you had seen Zeljko Bosnjak, and he was a member of the Convicts Battalion. Did you know Zeljko Bosnjak before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just superficially, because he used to install poker machines in coffee bars and things like that so I knew him from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And how did you learn that he was a member of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were at Siroki Brijeg, I saw him when we worked on a canal, I saw him along with Tuta, and we knew that he was a colonel with the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And now you may go ahead with what happened at the -- in the area of Ministry of Defence, when you saw Tuta.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Tuta, Misic, Juka, and Primorac were at the head of the column where there was a member of the army who had to carry a picture of Sefer Halilovic which was given to him personally by Juka. And then Tuta, holding a Motorola in his hand, hit this person whose name I don't want to mention now. He hit him in the face. He broke his Motorola against his face, and the man was all bloodied. Misic then jumped in and started to curse our balijas mothers, saying that we had killed his son. And then general chaos ensued. The ones who were -- who had been standing to the side started beating anybody in the column. Misic pulled out his pistol and shot around. Juka Prazina also jumped in, and I believe Primorac as well, and said that he had promised us that we would not be touched. Then Tuta said, verbatim, "Take this to Siroki and execute them." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They placed us on a bus, which had been prepared previously. They led us in, and Juka took the man who had been hit by Tuta with Motorola and placed him in his car, so he never went with us to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Will you stop here, Witness. And now we should clarify some questions. You just explained to the Trial Chamber that one of the persons you saw in the area of the ministry was Tuta.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know him before? Did you see him before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only by sight, yes, but I did used to see him. At Cim. That was a well-known restaurant, that is where I had seen him before. And I knew that that was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I think that we should go into private session for some minutes because the witness did not give us a name of a person who was hit by Tuta. I think that you will need this name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's just dwell a little bit on Tuta. Can you describe him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Shortish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: At the moment you saw him, how he looked like that moment. That's what I want to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I didn't -- how did he look? He looked angry, but he was shortish with a beard, skinny, very characteristic looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Was he dressed in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of uniform was on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did he have patches, badges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were very afraid. We did not look out for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And did you notice how the people surrounding him were treating him, were treating Tuta? I mean, how did they address him? Did they pronounce any military rank or something like that, or his name or something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I must object to the suggestive and leading question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a suggestive and leading question, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay, the first question was how the people surrounding Tuta were treating him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived, the men around Tuta were all expectant. They wanted to see what he was going to do. Nobody addressed him because he immediately started to shout and he hit this person whom I had named. So nobody addressed him in any way. Everybody was just waiting to see what he was going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Since the witness gave a response, I withdraw my two questions about the rank and the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know Tuta's real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mladen Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Now, go ahead with the MUP station in Siroki Brijeg. Had you ever been there before you were taken there on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. When they brought us there in the bus, they parked it in front of the MUP building. Juka Prazina's fighters were there with us, who had come in the bus with us. They lined us up. And the civilian police also came out and they stood behind these Juka's fighters, because it was clear that Juka's people were the ones in command. And then passers-by, who were passing by there because there were buildings around, and they were in uniforms, they started beating us. This went on for about 15 or 20 minutes. And then the police took us in, inside the building. They took away our belts. We had to take everything out of our pockets and leave it at the entrance. They took us to the basement, where there were two -- actually there were three solitary cells, but they first Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. filled up one and then the rest of them were brought into the second cell. When we entered, I found there two gentlemen who, according to the story that they told us, had come there the day before. I know their names. I do not want to mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for some seconds, maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know who was in command, in charge, of MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. A man who came in camouflage uniform and who called himself Cane, and he was with the Convicts Battalion. He was the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And who were the guards in MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards were civilian police who clearly were -- did not have command over the prison because two hours after we were brought there, we were branded as the men from the Vranica, and men in camouflage and black and other uniforms started arriving. The police was obliged to open the doors to our cells. They came in and beat us randomly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was personally beaten by Romeo Blazevic, B-l-a-z-e-v-i-c, and Darko Dodig also came with him, D-o-d-i-g, and a waiter whose first name was Vinko, and I don't know his last name. That was at Siroki Brijeg. They beat people in my cell, then they moved on to the next cell, and they continued with the beating there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know to which units all those people you just gave us in your testimony belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Romeo Blazevic, from what we heard, was a member of the Mostar ATG group, which was part of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Darko Dodig?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know to which group he belonged exactly. I also saw him later, during other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of food did you receive in MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received one tin per six people. I think it was something like 200 grams, and a quarter of a loaf of bread per day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they take you outside of MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Three or four days later, we were taken to a swimming pool which was perhaps 700 or 800 metres away from the MUP building, and we were to start clearing it, taking out the rocks that were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see Tuta at that time in the area of the swimming pool?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did see Tuta. Since the man who was in charge of the swimming pool was one of Tuta's fighting men, nicknamed Jablanica, Tuta would come to carry out an inspection, oversee the works, see how it's coming along, and on one occasion, he came together with Colonel Bosnjak. They didn't beat us or touch us at all then. And after that we stayed for just another four days. Since on the seventh day we got a very harsh beating from Cikota, five men from our room, from my room, and four men from the next room, were taken out one by one to a room in the basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe that the question was very simply: Did he see Mr. Naletilic? He answered that question. And now he is being non-responsive to the question and I object to the non-responsive nature of the answer at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, would you please guide your witness to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you very much. But I could not stop the witness since he is willing to narrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You mentioned now Cikota. Do you know -- did you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know it then. I learned it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: When did you learn his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he left that evening, the policemen who were taking us to wash ourselves told us the name of the man who had visited. There were another three men from the Convicts Battalion present, together with him. And the policemen then identified him for us. That's when I learned his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know to which unit he belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. How did you know that? How did you learn it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that day by the policemen, and then he told us about it himself. He told us various stories, both good and bad, involving the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, Witness, since you were stopped by my learned colleague, I would like to ask the question. What happened in the basement when you were taken one by one from your cell and, according to your testimony, there was a harsh beating from Cikota? Could you dwell a little bit on this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Before myself, he took out two men one by one. I was the third in line. I don't know what the criteria were. When I got out, a man about whom I later learned that he was from Rijeka was standing beside Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. him. On the right-hand side, on a bench, there was an older plump man sitting, and then Cikota started kicking me. Since he's tall, lanky, and long-legged, he started kicking me and beating me on the head. And then he handcuffed me to the banister of the stairs leading into that area. He extinguished two cigarettes on my tongue and forced me to swallow them, never stopping the beating and the kicking. All of this lasted for about 15 minutes. And then he put me back in the cell after which he moved to another cell and started taking people out from there. The next day, Cane, the warden of the prison, came and said that the best thing for us would be to transfer to Ljubuski, which was about 15 or 20 kilometres away. And indeed, the next day, in the afternoon, we were transferred on a bus to the Ljubuski prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I just asked you about Cikota's first name, but I don't see the response in the transcript. Maybe you didn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Hrkac is his name, and the nickname is Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed with Ljubuski now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought to Ljubuski in the evening at dusk, and we were by then 36. 33 of us brought from Mostar, plus two men who were already there, plus another man, a professor, from Mostar who was brought just with his socks on his feet, with his jaw swollen, who told us that he had been beaten and brought, according to his own words, by Stela and his men, Stela personally. The 36 of us were taken to a cell which was about 5 metres long, perhaps even less, about a metre 20, metre 30 wide. And we calculated that we had about 33 square centimetres per person. We slept standing up. Of course, you can't call it sleeping. We stood up the whole night because we couldn't even crouch for lack of space. The next day, we were only taken out once, for lunch. And there we were given pork paste, which most of us didn't want to eat. In the evening, we were taken out again, taken outside to get some air. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please, Mr. President and Your Honours, I apologise. But I'm looking at line 8 on page 21, and it wasn't even a question. It was just, May we proceed to Ljubuski. So my objection would be there's no question in front of this witness, number one; and number two, if there was a question, he has become nonresponsive at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the witness is quite responsive concerning the situation in Ljubuski, but it is really not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: There was a question, what happened in Ljubuski? I just told the witness, just what happened in Ljubuski and proceed with Ljubuski. What kind of question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you have to phrase your question in the form of a question, so that at least it will give some guidance to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, how were you treated in Ljubuski by the persons who were in charge of the camp and other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already said, we were taken to isolation cells, or rather one isolation cell, all 36 of us. There was no space to even crouch or to sit down. The door was closed, and the small window on the door was also closed. Since it is an old building and there are cracks in the wall in corners, the only air we got was from those cracks. The first time we were allowed to go out was the next day for lunch, and then we were given only half an hour. And after that, as men from Vranica, we no longer had any right to leave the cell. The next day, we were taken out. We were allowed to get out alone, only us, without the other prisoners. We remained outside for ten minutes before we were brought back again. We were taken out again for lunch. I don't remember what we had, but it was some sort of lentils or peas. There were people from Sovici and Jablanica and other places, and there were people from Mostar, some of them soldiers. Others were civilians. In the afternoon, several of us were taken out, and then came -- then arrived Ernest Takac, then a man with a last name of Peric, then Pehar, nicknamed Dolma, and they started beating us with all sorts of things. There were thick electric cables tied one to another, seven centimetres thick or thereabouts, and that's what they beat us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you know from which unit Ernest Takac was and also another -- the second person, Pehar, whose nickname was Dolma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to others, it's a group that was established in Mostar, and I think they too belonged to the ATG, the anti-terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent another night there. And the next day, around noon, there arrived Jablanica, accompanied by another two men. There was Medic, whose father owned a well-known restaurant in Mostar before the war, and there was another man in his entourage, and they had arrived to take 18 of us to Siroki Brijeg again to finish work on the swimming pool and other works.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, would you please ask your question again? Because we don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you just gave -- given the name of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel speak into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [No microphone] ... swimming pool?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He came to fetch us back, because the swimming pool wasn't finished. We had worked on it for about four days before going to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... which unit he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So, witness, I would like usher to place Exhibit P26.10 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the swimming pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What does this picture depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This here is the swimming pool on which we worked. First of all, we removed the stones, and then we cleared the shrubbery around it, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then we cleared a small brook on this side, through which the water flows and fills the pool. The boss here was Jablanica, whom I mentioned before. Tuta arrived across this bridge. He would go around, inspect, together with Jablanica, because the guards who were guarding us said that the two of them together were going to turn it into sports and recreation grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... exhibit away. Witness BB, you were taken, according to your witness statement, testimony, you were taken just to the swimming pool and where were you detained at that time? I mean after Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent only three days in prison, and then we were transferred to the Tobacco Institute, which was the quarters of the Convicts Battalion command. And there we were put in a sort of hut, for our own safety, as they said, because the guards who were guarding us were from the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... P26.9 on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think you have to wait until the translation finishes. For several times, we cannot get translation. We only catch half of your sentence in the transcript, and you have to speak into the microphone. I understand there is some problem with this mic, but you have to be very careful to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I will try to fix it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, had you ever been in Siroki Brijeg before you were taken there on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In passing, yes. I passed through Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what the picture on the ELMO means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the old Tobacco Institute where we were imprisoned in this building here, more precisely the lower half of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Which building do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Behind this building, you can see a red roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, just the building --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This building is outside the fence of the Tobacco Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just outside this building, just outside, it doesn't belong to the perimeter of the Tobacco Institute. This red roof here in the lower half of the building were us prisoners, and the other half belonged to the so-called Poskok battalion. Half of this prefab building belonged to them; and in the other half, we were kept. This here --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean the small building with the red roof as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- this is Tuta's command. Because we went there to paint the walls of the upstairs rooms, because Tuta was supposed to move in upstairs. We washed the carpets, cleaned the windows, and we prepared it for his moving in. There was an incident on one occasion, two of his men got into a fight, and he got out to see what the noise was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, just take a marker, please, and indicate with number 1 the building where you were kept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just with a number 1, the building where you were kept, mark with marker. Number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, and now with number 2, the building where, according to your testimony, Tuta's headquarters were located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. And I see that there is a -- one construction which just reminds me of the swimming pool. Is it the same swimming pool you were working? I mean, just to the right side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the swimming pool, the same swimming pool on which we had worked from the fourth day of our arrival onwards. This is the swimming pool. This is the bridge that we used to cross. Here was the auxiliary entrance through which we got in in order to avoid crossing the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please mark it with number 3. Swimming pool.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you finish your job on the swimming pool?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: You may take away the exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know we worked on it for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Were you involved in some other jobs while you were kept in the Tobacco Institute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Tobacco Institute, while we were there, people came. When we were returned, the day after our return, even Cikota came to take us to his own house to chop wood for two days. Those were the first two days while we were still in prison, not at the Tobacco Institute. After that, we went in groups of three, four, five men to various houses. I went to Mamici together with three other men to take down a wall, dig. Then we went to Posusje, did some work in a big storage house. It was a storage of footwear and food. And we arranged it. We also worked in the storage facility of the Poskok battalion. And as far as Cikota's house is concerned, I worked there for about a month, not in a row but for five days -- for five-day intervals. Some men went to work in Zeljko Bosnjak's house. When you get out of Mostar -- towards Mostar from Siroki Brijeg, that's the place where he had started to build the house. I can't remember exactly now. In July, we started digging a canal, as we later realised about 500 metres from Tuta's house towards the main road, and in the direction of the water supply reservoir. With interruptions, we worked throughout July and August, 13 of us, with another group of about 10 to 12 men, prisoners, who were kept in the school building near Brkovic -- sorry, Dobrkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, could we stop here? Because it's time for the break, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to check with you in one issue, just if you look at paragraph 28, line 5, of the transcript, where you were talking about some school building. I would like to clarify the name of this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. school building, because it's -- I can't make it out from our transcript. Could you repeat the name of that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dobrkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you spell it, please? It's not an easy name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: D-o-b-r-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Dobrkovic. Thank you. So, witness, you've just claimed that you were working just not far from Tuta's house. How did you learn that the house you were talking about belonged to Tuta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we worked there, I saw Tuta on two occasions coming out of the door of that building, to the side of where our bus was parked. They used to bus us in, and the civilian policemen were escorting us. On one occasion, it was parked near the gate and Tuta came out and started yelling at the driver and the policemen because they had parked too close. And on subsequent days, we stepped -- we would step off the bus 300 metres before the house, and the guards, who were members of the Convicts Battalion and those who guarded us were home guards, they told us that that was Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you work inside of the house itself or not? I mean Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever approach that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because it was fenced off. Actually, there was a wall, a stone wall, on both sides of the gate, and we passed about 30 metres away from that wall. From that vantage point, you could only see a portion of the roof of the house. We could see the house from the street on the other side, when we were going around. When we were going to the Dobrkovic school, that is the side from which you could see the house. And the guards identified it as Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of job did you perform while working on the construction site of the canal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a hill, I don't know, 100, 150 metres elevation, and we dug a canal, breaking the rock by the roadside, and it was about -- once it was finished, it was about 300 metres long, and it was about one metre wide and one metre deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How many hours per day did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would leave in the morning, around 8.00, and then we were there until 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did anyone pay you for your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody paid us. And the food that we were getting over there at this prefab building where we slept consisted of two slices of bread and some jam. Then we would bring that along. The first five days, the food was being delivered there. We also received a little -- some water, three, two-litre bottles for a group of 20 to 25 of us. And this was during the month of August, when the temperatures are very high. So there you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you communicate with prisoners from Dobrkovic school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We talked because we were working together on that canal, and as I said, there were between sometime 10, sometime 12, sometime 15, depended on the day, and the 13 of us made about 25 in total each day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they tell you in what conditions they were kept in Dobrkovic detention facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They talked about it. They slept on the floor. They had blankets which they used for a pillow. And because they were guarded by the home guards, they themselves called themselves the home guards, men in uniform could come and beat us, and this happened. And also they were being hit with tinned food which they kept, they tried to hide. Sometimes they would get it in the morning and they hid it in order to eat it at a later time, so they were beaten by -- hit with these. And we could see that because they were taking off their T-shirts and shirts because of the heat, and we could see the black-and-blue marks on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they tell you who was beating them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They, themselves, did not know at first who was coming in a red Porsche until we told them that this person's name was Ivan Hrkac, called Cikota. And he always had with him at least one other fighter in uniform who also mistreated -- took part in the mistreatment. One day, when we were coming back from work, and they would leave earlier, we saw down there some commotion in front of the school building. We also saw a car which drove away. Our driver was told to immediately take us away, not to linger on. And the next day, they told us that even Cikota had come. And a person who was skilled in karate, they had taken out a teacher. This karate person kicked him in the chest, and the man died.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that man who died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because he did not beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It seems to me that you haven't understood my question. I'm just asking you about the person who, according to the Dobrkovic prisoners, died after the beating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was Professor Krilic, K-r-i-l-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know who was in charge of Dobrkovic detention facilities? Did they tell you, I mean prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Who was in charge of your detention facilities in the Tobacco Institute area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Why do you think so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because at first, only members of the Convicts Battalion could enter there. Later on, the fighters of the Poskok Battalion were also able to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: And how did they treat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards who guarded us were from the Convicts Battalion, and some of them even showed us some identity cards. And apparently by certain numbers, digits, you could tell that they were from that battalion. And some guards, when they arrived, when some individuals in uniform would come, the three guards, because there were three per shift, they could open -- unlock the doors, and we were spread over three rooms where we slept. Then they would unlock the door, and then whoever would want to come in would come in and beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever see Tuta in your detention facilities? I mean in the Tobacco Institute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we painted his offices on the top floor when he was supposed to move in there. He came to see how the work was progressing, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and we saw him from the window. I saw him twice with Stela. And I saw him also when he came out to calm down the two of his men, the two guards who had an altercation, and they were the guards who were guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did any other of the KB - I mean the Convicts Battalion - unit ever visit the detention facilities? I mean -- sorry. Did any other commander, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 78th days -- because this is how I memorized events, by the days, because we counted. On the 78th day, Colonel Andabak came with two fighters of the Convicts Battalion. I know that one of them was nicknamed "Robija." I don't know the name of the other one. He was shorter. There were three of us sleeping in one cell. I would not like to divulge their names right now. He took out one of them. Ten minutes later, he took out the next one, and I had to step out of the room and be by the door. I could hear the moans, and then it was my turn as third. He made me sit down in a chair against the wall. To the left was Robija, that is that man named Robija, and the other man was on the other side. And then he identified himself as Colonel Andabak, Tuta's deputy. He asked insignificant things, insignificant to me, that is. Where was the safe that the army had? Where was the money that was kept in the basement? And I was in no position to know any of this. I did not know whether there was any safe or any money. After each question was accompanied by a blow, by either of the two men who were standing next to me. They were either kicks or punches. That went on for about ten minutes, and then we were led out and taken to another room where we were joined with the others. Four or five days later, two men came, one identified himself as commander -- actually, as a SIS operative, and the other one as a VOS operative, V-O-S. This took place about ten days after one of those who were with us in the prison was released. He was released and taken to Makarska and released to his father, as we were told by Colonel Zeljko Bosnjak, because it was he himself who took him there. They came again for the three of us, because the three of us were still together, and we were taken out one by one to another room. They threatened us with a pistol. They put a pistol in our mouth. They hit us, and asked how much money Zeljko Bosnjak got. We had no idea this man would be released or Zeljko Bosnjak would get any money for it. We just did not have any knowledge of that. After that, for two days, we received no food. We stopped being taken to work. We remained locked up in the room, and occasionally we would be allowed to go to the toilet. And that went on for 10 to 15 days. And then we went to some factory to dig a canal and to place some cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you know Andabak before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you describe his appearances now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform, not very tall, a round face with spectacles, and hair that wasn't very long, not cut military style but not very long either. If I saw a picture of him, I would recognise him immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, in your testimony today, you have mentioned the name of a person whose name was Stela. Did you know that person before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from Balinovac, from Balinovac, which is a neighbourhood in Mostar where I played soccer. And so I've known Stela for over 25 years. But we never really socialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see him during the war? I mean apart from those two occasions when you saw him at Stela's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Him personally? No. Just in passing in Mostar, in a car, because he had very characteristic-looking car. The colour of his car could be described as pink panther. It was an American-built car, a Chevrolet, a convertible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know which position he occupied during the war? I mean the war in 1993, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the -- to his fighters, he was a commander of the ATG group, which was part of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that, that his unit was a part of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 17th or 19th of September, we were released from the camp to two men with cars, who took us to Mostar. We arrived in Mostar at the Rondo, the four of us, and there we were in front and behind the building where Radio Mostar was. There is a yard there and we were -- we were sitting there, and the police asked us where did we come from? And the young man who guarded us said that he was a member of the Convicts Battalion in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But did he tell you to which unit he belonged to? What was the name of the unit he was enlisted in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That unit was part of the Convicts Battalion, because he showed the policemen an identity card, because the policeman did -- left us alone after that, which to me meant that he was above the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I think that now we should go into private session for some minutes because you remember the witness did not give names of people who were beaten along with him in tobacco station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole night and the whole next day, we were carrying large amounts of explosive, which had been transported to the front of the restaurant nearby. And we carried it to a manhole near the Lenin park, the Lenin promenade. And we carried these explosives through the manhole to a place near the court building on the other side road, a section held by the BH army. It was 1600 kilos of explosive that we carried over. And since the four of us couldn't manage it on our own, another six prisoners were brought, and they worked in Santic Street that night to get it carried over by the next day. I know it's exactly 1600 kilos because I went to Rudnik together with one of the soldiers to bring the tools necessary for opening the manhole because the manhole had been closed. And then we stopped by a place where a man was loading explosives on to a truck. He said there would be 2400 kilos. And since our guard, Jure Djidic was not accompanying us, he told me to get it myself. And when we had done it, the man said, "Tell the driver it's only 1600, not more." That's how I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness BB, do you know for which unit you were performing this job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit, the group which was located there and headed by a man whom I only know by his nickname, Tange, because he was the owner of the Tange Lange Cafe. That's how he got his nickname. There was also a man named Vili, son of Suljo, who was also well known in Zagreb. There was also Jure Djidic, and there was a man who used to be the goalkeeper of the Locomotiva team. And they all belonged to what they called an independent sabotage group attached to the Convicts Battalion. That's what they said. That's what Tange personally told us that morning while we were drying ourselves because we were wet from working in the sewage manhole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Did they tell the name of the unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man Willy said that they were a sabotage group, but he didn't say more than that. It was Tange who said they were attached to the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, I would like the usher to place Exhibit Number 14.3 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Please, Witness, could you indicate in this picture the place you were performing your job with explosives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Can you mark it, please -- yes, first the pointer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here on this picture, you can't see the manhole through which we carried the explosive because it's in the street which goes down below the edge of the picture. From this corner here, it's about 7 to 8 metres in the middle of the road. We carried it through the sewage which goes along here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, you may take a marker and just indicate the route you were carrying explosives to. To begin with, the building just to the left side, do you know the name of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is Aleksa Santic High School. This is the third primary school. They switched places at one point, so this used to be the high school and this used to be the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now, you can put number 1 on this building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But I don't see the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Aleksa Santic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO because we cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Aleksa Santic High School, and this is the third primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Put number 2 on the primary school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our route started here at the manhole, and it crossed this way right here. From this point, we turned in the direction of this building, and then we went here below. This here was the first manhole where we left explosives --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near the building of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would like the usher to put Exhibit Number 39.1 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Witness BB, could you identify someone -- anyone on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Could you show this person with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Put a number 1, because there are two persons here in the photo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Oh, my God. You have overdone it. Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: So Witness BB identified a person marked with number 1 as Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I've got a couple more questions. While talking about Ljubuski, Witness, you said that you had been beaten by Ernest Takac and Pehar, whose nickname was Dolma. Do you know to which unit they belonged? Who was their commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They belonged to the same group as Romeo Blazevic, who belonged to Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From their own words, the Convicts Battalion was established in Mostar to defend Mostar, and that's where this ATG, anti-terrorist group, came in, and also this sabotage group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But what was -- what is the link between the sabotage group and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Stela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ATG was not established during the war between Croats and Muslims. It was established before. Juka had his own unit, and in the same way, this side had its own. And rumour had it, in cafes and places, that the commander was Stela. Many boasted that they were members of that group, just as Takac boasted of it, the same as Dolma, Romeo. They bragged themselves that they were fighting men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you released from the detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late in October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness. Your Honour, my examination-in-chief is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you did a very good job, that you finished with this witness with your direct examination within the time frame you told us. Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. If you would be just kind enough to have the ELMO lowered to begin with so I can see the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Let me introduce myself. I am Defence counsel for the accused Mr. Naletilic, and I will be putting to you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, when did you transfer to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't in the BH army for even a day. I was in the 4th Battalion, and I do have my soldier's ID, and it's also in the computer. You can check. I was in the group for maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. But please answer just briefly my questions. You've told me that you were not there, and that's it. You didn't have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You spent your nights in Vranica as a simple civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I took over the apartment of a Serb person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You took it over yourself or somebody gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I took it over myself because the apartment where I used to live was destroyed by shells and I had nowhere to sleep. Everybody took over other people's apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you give any oath, for instance, in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because I was mobilised during the general mobilisation to the northern camp. I was taken to the northern camp and to the Tihomir Misic camp. That's where the mobilisation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were there any -- was there any fighting before the 9th in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean before the 9th of May? Yes, there was fighting on the 16th and 17th of April, 1993, around the Mostar Hotel and around the high school. There were police forces and the army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know of any agreements made between the HVO and the BH army as to who would be stationed where and who would draw lines, before the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One evening, I was in my apartment, because I was overlooking that place, as I said before. I heard noise down below. I went to the window, and I saw Arif Pasalic, nicknamed Hujko -- Arif Pasalic, sorry, and Hujko having an argument, and Pasalic told Hujko that they had just signed an agreement and that they should move their police, I don't know where. I heard it with my own ears because I was six or seven metres above them. It was night-time and it was quiet all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you tell this Court who is Arif Pasalic and who is Hujko, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arif Pasalic is the corps commander of the BH army, and Hujko is the commander of the BH army brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is that the well-known 1st Mostar Brigade commanded by Hujdur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what number that brigade was. I just know that he was the commander of one of those brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was that argument because -- was that argument over one of them wanting to comply with the agreement and the other not wanting to, or was it about something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the chain of command that I was taught in school, corps commander is superior to the brigade commander. And the brigade commander, as far as I could see, was not present in that meeting, and this other one was informing him. That's how I understood that scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I seem to have heard you saying, and that's what came -- what's in the transcript. You said that they had an argument. An argument is not the passing of information. An argument is a quarrel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was an argument that didn't awaken the whole highrise, but it did wake me up and perhaps another person on the floor above. And one man was saying to the other that he should submit to him, that he should comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, and please confirm or otherwise, there was a quarrel between Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Hujko because one of them didn't want to submit to the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a quarrel. It was an argument. I said it was an argument. It is a much milder expression and a much milder type of talk than a quarrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, do you know whether Mr. -- I'll speak more slowly now for the transcript. Did Mr. Mithad Hujdur -- no, it's not right. M-i-t-h-a-d H-u-j-d-u-r.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to know what my learned colleague is leading to, because I don't think it is relevant to the case or the charges against his client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I also would like to know this question. Mr. Krsnik, could you give us an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you would bear with me for another minute, you will learn the answer. I don't want to explain in front of the witness why I'm putting a certain question. That's one. And I would also be very grateful, Your Honour, because we have also general background in this indictment, and this question is very relevant, especially what the witness was talking about right now. And when you hear the next question, you will understand the meaning of the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you remember giving any statements to the representatives of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this Court except for testifying today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you give any statements to the investigators of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a complete report, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you gave them a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally, I have given a statement to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you remember when and to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was about two years ago, I believe. And I especially don't remember to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: During that questioning, were you telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you said all you knew, and you answered their questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I will say the same to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just a minute, just a minute. In that statement, you stated that on the 7th and the 8th of April, you were in the BH army. And on the evening of the 8th of April, you were defending the high school and the Mostar Hotel. However, you had to turn them over to the Croatian army as a result of the agreement reached between Pero Zelenika, on the one hand, and General Pasalic on the other hand. Today, you said you had never been in the BH army. That's the reason for my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't. I wasn't in the army even then. You should know that at that time, some better-known fighters from the army made a group to defend this area around the park, so it was not joining the army. It was just fighters on their own initiative, just as some people from the HVO. And I joined that group that evening because it was an attempt to avoid the conflict and to prevent the conflict between the army and the HVO. I was there that evening, but I wasn't a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you said in your statement, "When the HVO attack started, I joined the BH army." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to observe all our rules, I can present the witness with this document. My colleagues also have this statement in both versions. May I ask the usher to give the witness this statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's no need to. I know it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: To refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then you went on to say, "I'm a Bosniak Muslim. I wanted to defend my city. We were deployed by Hujka -- that is, we were deployed by Hujka, who is the commander of the Mostar Brigade of BH army. On 7 April, 1993, during the night, I was in the big park in front of the Mostar Hotel and the grammar school. The distance between these two buildings is about 200 metres. I was together with another 80 soldiers of the BH army. We wanted to defend the two aforementioned buildings. The BH army was informed about the attack two or three days in advance. I know this. I cannot tell you who passed on that information." Were you with the BH army or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So what is stated there -- here is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This is mistranslated. I am a Bosniak from -- I'm a citizen of Mostar. I did not say I was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Bosniak Muslim or Bosniak Mostar man, I respect whatever you want to say, the way -- however you feel yourself to be, but the rest of it, did you say the rest of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So let me ask you again. So were you a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was never a member of the ABiH, but as a born Mostar man, like others who were not members of ABiH, who had come there, we all knew about the attack. We wanted to prevent it. Other people came from outside, to that park, on the HVO side. There were no local Mostar men in that park that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you look at the paragraph before? "In the evening of 8 April, 1993, we defended the grammar school and the Mostar Hotel." So that was the question which I asked you previously. So now you have it in front of you. And I continue: "But we had to give them to the Croatian side because of the agreement between General Pasalic, as representative of the Muslim side, and Pero Zelenika, as an HVO representative." In the evening of 8 April, did you sleep peacefully at home or were you defending these sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack was between 8.00 and 10.00 in the evening, and then we all went home because the soldiers who did not know this area left the park and [redacted] [redacted], at least those of us who came out to help that night in order to avoid the conflict. It was then that I heard -- and this was midnight by this time, when this took place, between Pasalic and Pero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You now said that you were there defending the grammar school and the Mostar Hotel, and then in the next paragraph, you describe -- this would be -- let's go on to the next paragraph. "The attack lasted for two hours. The HVO soldiers did not expect BH army soldiers in the park after their attack and subsequent escape from the park. We left and I went home." My question is: Were you, as a member of the ABiH, in the park when this attack took place, then you chased the HVO soldiers, as you said, and then you went home to sleep? Is that what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as a member of the army. As many men from Mostar, who did not belong to any army, we came there to defend these places as members of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We've heard that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I was not a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When I asked you today earlier, you said that you did not have any weapons. How did you defend that park?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said in the 4th Battalion, I never -- I was never issued any type of weapons before or later. I found my own uniform --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That was not my question and that was not your answer. My question was, were you a member of ABiH; you said no. And I asked you whether you had any weapons; and you said no. I asked you, did you sleep in that apartment as a civilian; and you said yes. That was today. And now, I ask you today, did you have any weapon that night? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night, yes. That was the only night I had, and I never denied that. I also had a personal pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of weapon did you have that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean that night?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is that the AK-47?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I know it's called Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is that a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A submachine-gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was a rifle, an automatic rifle. A Kalashnikov is an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Kalashnikov is an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is not a submachine-gun. There is a big difference in calibre. I know that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you had this Kalashnikov in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
